
Overview
Rotator cuff disease is a broad classification of pathology, with its natural history ranging
from tendinitis to rotator cuff arthropathy. As disease progresses, properties of the
tendon change, contributing to further degradation and symptoms experienced by the
patient. An understanding of the natural history of rotator cuff disease and the basic
science involved in tendon tears, repairs, and healing will allow surgeons to have
informed discussions with patients regarding treatment, help surgeons determine
treatment type, and allow surgeons to use mechanical and biologic strategies to improve
tendon healing and clinical outcomes.
Anatomy of the Rotator Cuff
Vascular Anatomy
The major arterial supply of the rotator cuff includes the ascending branch of the anterior
humeral circumflex artery, the acromial branch of the thoracoacromial artery, the
suprascapular artery, and the posterior humeral circumflex artery (Figure 1).
Altered blood supply and changes in vascularity may cause tears in the rotator cuff tendon.1
The blood supply has major effects on tendon quality, tendon degeneration, and tendon
healing.
Extraneous factors and conditions that affect microvascular status have a subsequent effect
on the rotator cuff condition and healing.
The hypovascular critical zone of the rotator cuff is located on the articular side, close to its
insertion on the greater tuberosity.
Studies have shown that total blood flow in the rotator cuff is greater with intact tendons than
with a torn tendon.2

Vascular Anatomy
Blood flow is important to tendon health and disease. Poor vascularity is associated with
tendon degeneration and poor tendon healing. Most importantly, it affects tendon-to-
bone remodeling potential and healing. As patients age, the vascularity of the rotator

tears and greater difficulty in healing with aging. Similarly, conditions that decrease
vascularity, such as the vasoconstrictive effects of nicotine and the negative effects of
hypercholesterolemia and diabetes mellitus, may contribute to rotator cuff degeneration
and poorer healing capacity after surgical repair.
Specific regions of relative avascularity between the vascular zones, also known as
watershed regions, are at risk of rupture and have been identified in the supraspinatus.3
This likely corresponds with the rotator crescent, which is the most common site of
initiation of rotator cuff tears.4
Neural Anatomy
Free nerve endings are clustered at the enthesis, which is responsible for nociception.
Other nerve endings, such as those responsible for proprioception, stretch, and vibration,
mostly are in the myotendinous region.

Neural Anatomy
Because the enthesis is the primary site of nociceptive pain fibers, some evidence
suggests this is the reason midsubstance tears may be less painful/symptomatic than
tears that occur at the bone-tendon junction. If proprioception is not restored, tendon
repair outcomes are diminished.3 The absence of shoulder pain in many patients with a
degenerative rotator cuff tear suggests that structures other than the tendon (ie,
inflamed bursal tissue) may be responsible for shoulder pain.
Tendons
Tendons allow the transmission of force from muscle to bone, and they provide dynamic joint
stability via mechanical, viscoelastic, and proprioceptive properties.5

Rotator cuff tendons are flat, not round, which makes them better for high tensile loads and
complex loads, such as compression and shear.3
Tendons are made up of water, collagen, and proteoglycans.
Tendon structure: triple helix collagen → microfibril → fibril → fascicle → tendon (Figure 2)
Tendons have two primary junctions: the myotendinous junction and the enthesis.
Some debate exists about the exact dimensions of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus
tendons, which blend together to insert into the superior and posterior aspect of the greater
tuberosity.6
Contributions of the subscapularis and supraspinatus footprints are critical for stabilization of
the long head of the biceps tendon as it enters the glenohumeral joint.

Tendons
The material properties of tendons allow them to elastically store and transfer energy.
Tendons demonstrate viscous properties at low loads and more elastic properties with
higher loads. Maximum tensile stress occurs on the articular side of the supraspinatus
toward its anterior edge. Most of the stress placed on the tendon occurs at the bone-

tendon junction. The main functional components of tendons are water and collagen.
The collagen that makes up tendon structure is mostly type I (95%) and a small amount
of type III.3 Proteoglycans, such as decorin and biglycan, contribute to the structure of
tendons and tenocytes. Decorin is responsible for tendon size and is associated with
tension-bearing regions. Aggrecan and biglycan are more abundant in areas of
compression, such as the anterior region of the supraspinatus.5
The hierarchy of tendon structure consists initially of a collagen triple helix, which
together forms a microfibril. Many microfibrils together form a fibril, which then makes
up fascicles. Multiple fascicles form the final tendon structure. The myotendinous
portion consists of myofilament bundles that insert directly into the collagen fibrils of the
tendon. The enthesis also is known as the bone-tendon junction. Tendon inserts into
bone via direct insertions with a four-layer transition: tendon, fibrocartilage, mineralized
fibrocartilage, and bone. These layers have a linear increase of mineral to collagen ratio.
At this junction, a sharp transitory gradient occurs from tendon to bone, which increases
focal stress at this location.7
The medial-lateral width has been described as 12 to 14 mm; therefore, tears that are 6
to 7 mm medial-lateral correspond with 50% partial-thickness tears, which is important
in determining if débridement or repair is the best treatment option.
Original descriptions of tendon insertion anatomy described the supraspinatus footprint
as 13 mm in width medial-lateral and 20 mm anterior to posterior. The infraspinatus
footprint measured 14 mm wide and 20 mm superoinferior.6 More recently, anatomic
descriptions of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus footprints changed. Mochizuki et al8
described the supraspinatus footprint as triangular in shape with a broader medial
anteroposterior dimension of 12.6 mm and a smaller lateral anteroposterior dimension
of 1.3 mm, with 21% of specimens also inserting into the upper aspect of the lesser
tuberosity. The infraspinatus footprint was described as trapezoidal in shape sweeping
lateral to the traditional supraspinatus insertion and providing a larger footprint
insertion measuring 20.2 mm in length medially and 32.7 mm laterally (Figure 3).

coracohumeral ligaments contribute to the formation of a sheath that envelops the

Musculature
Four muscles make up the rotator cuff: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and
subscapularis (Figure 4).
The rotator cuff tendons insert just distal to the joint, allowing it to act as a buttress against
translation.

glenoid, further augmenting the dynamic stability of the glenohumeral joint.

Musculature
The subscapularis is located anteriorly, supraspinatus is located superiorly, and the
infraspinatus and teres minor are located posteriorly. Each muscle provides a force
across the shoulder that corresponds to their direction of pull, together providing
balance and dynamic stability to the joint. Progressive rotator cuff tears weaken the
shoulder and alter the biokinematics of the shoulder joint by disrupting these force
couples.

Cable-Crescent Concept
The rotator cable is a thick bundle of fibers that run perpendicular to the tendon fibers
connecting the supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendons.
The rotator cable is critical to structural and functional cuff integrity, providing a stress-
shielded area in the center of the cuff, termed the rotator crescent (Figure 5).
Figure 5 Illustrations show that a rotator cuff tear has a similar configuration to a suspension
bridge and can be modeled after the loaded cable of the bridge. The free margin of the tear
corresponds to the cable, and the anterior and posterior attachments of the tear correspond
to the supports at each end of the cable’s span. (Reproduced with permission from Burkhart
SS, Esch JC, Jolson RS: The rotator crescent and rotator cable: An anatomic description of the
shoulder’s “suspension bridge.” Arthroscopy 1993;9[6]:611-616.)

Cable-Crescent Concept
Originally described by Burkhart et al,9 the rotator cable is a thickened horseshoe-
shaped region consisting of the anteriormost 8 to 12 mm of the supraspinatus,
spanning from the region just posterior to the biceps tendon to the inferior border of
the infraspinatus. The rotator cable is thought to shield the crescent from stress, in a
suspension-bridge model. As patients age, relative avascularity of the rotator crescent
leads to progressive thinning of the area, putting more strain on the rotator cable.4
Tears in the cable increase tear gap distance and strain compared with those in the
crescent. Cable-disrupted tears are larger at baseline.10 Similarly, tears involving the

Biomechanics of the Rotator Cuff
The subscapularis contributes to the anteroposterior rotator cuff force couple and provides a
direct barrier effect against anterior translation of the humeral head.
In the coronal plane, the anteroposterior rotator cuff force couple acts in concert to oppose
the translational pull of the deltoid muscle, helping to center the humeral head.
The infraspinatus and teres minor are the prime external rotators of the shoulder.

Biomechanics of the Rotator Cuff
The subscapularis is a strong internal rotator of the glenohumeral joints assisted by the
pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, and teres major. The primary function of the
subscapularis is to contribute to the anteroposterior force couple, along with the
posterior cuff, promoting humeral head centering and opposing the translational pull of
the deltoid muscle. Coordinated force couple activity also augments stability of the joint
through concavity-compression of the humeral head into the glenoid. In addition, the
subscapularis is an important direct restraint to anterior humeral head translation via a
barrier effect.
The supraspinatus muscle contributes to elevation motion and strength, especially in the
early arc of motion; however, isolated supraspinatus tears minimally reduce elevation
strength biomechanically and often are well tolerated functionally.12 The infraspinatus
and teres minor muscles are the primary external rotators of the glenohumeral joint
along with the posterior deltoid. Large posterior cuff tears that involve these muscles
may result in profound external rotation weakness and functional deficits for which very
limited compensatory capabilities exist.
Progressive disruption of the rotator cuff will result in elevation and external rotation
weakness. If the tear propagates into the infraspinatus, proximal humerus migration will

Epidemiology of Degenerative Rotator Cuff Tears
Impingement/cuff tendonitis to full-thickness rotator cuff tears represents a spectrum of
disease that begins with tendinitis (patients aged 20 to 35 years); progresses to tendinosis
(patients aged 35 to 45 years); and, potentially, rotator cuff tears (patients >45 years); and, if
not managed, evolves to cuff arthropathy (patients >65 years).
Atraumatic rotator cuff tears are part of the normal aging process. Depending on the study,
the prevalence ranges from 9.7% of patients younger than 20 years, to 28% of patients
younger than 50 years, to 65% of patients older than 70 years.

Epidemiology of Degenerative Rotator Cuff Tears
Most degenerative (atraumatic) rotator cuff tears are asymptomatic, with the major risk
factor related to age. Rotator cuff tears in younger overhead athletes commonly were
thought to occur near the confluence of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus, whereas
tears in older patients were typically thought to occur on the articular surface just
posterior to the biceps (age-related changes). However, recent studies have challenged
this notion, with natural history studies demonstrating that most degenerative tears are
located and likely originate more posterior to the biceps tendon, closer to the
supraspinatus/infraspinatus confluence within the rotator crescent.15
Age-associated increases in the prevalence of tears begin at age 50 years and increase
with each decade. Although partial-thickness tears are more common, the prevalence of
full-thickness rotator cuff tears is 7% to 40%, with most occurring in patients older than
55 years. For those older than 66 years with a symptomatic rotator cuff tear, the

Risk Factors

Risk Factors
The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons prognostic factor evidence summary
on the management of rotator cuff injuries separates modifiable and nonmodifiable
prognostic factors from formal treatment recommendations. These factors are most
useful for preoperative counseling, expectation setting, and optimization rather than
categorical denial of treatment.
Prognostic factors that may affect patient counseling, healing, retear risk,
complications, and patient-reported outcomes include patient age, body mass index,
tobacco/nicotine use, diabetes mellitus, comorbidity burden, patient expectations,
behavioral health, preoperative stiffness, worker’s compensation status, social
determinants of health, family history, and hypercholesterolemia.16,17
Other medical comorbidities, such as chronic kidney disease, may lead to in vivo
degradation of tendons.
Most prognostic factor evidence is low quality or conflicting; these factors should
guide shared decision making and optimization rather than serve as absolute
contraindications to rotator cuff repair if surgical management is otherwise
indicated.17
Advancing patient age is the primary risk factor for degenerative rotator cuff disease;
however, growing evidence also suggests genetic predisposition.18,19 Older patient age
is associated with higher failure rates and poorer patient-reported outcomes in some
studies; however, patient age alone should not be a contraindication to rotator cuff
repair because healing failure is multifactorial. As patients age, tendons demonstrate
decreased cellularity, increased apoptosis, increased fascicular thinning/disruption, and

increased granulation tissue. This correlates with a decreased ability to heal with age,
which also is affected by reduced bone quality and tendon vascularity. Older patients
tend to have greater fatty degeneration and tear retraction, which decreases the ability
of repair and healing. Nicotine affects the amount of collagen deposition and repair at
surgical wound sites because of vasoconstriction and, in several studies, has been
associated with poorer healing, increased retear rates, and inferior patient-reported
outcomes; however, not all studies report significant differences.17 Patients should be
counseled to stop tobacco and nicotine use, if possible.
Family history also has been attributed to an increased risk of rotator cuff tear. Evidence
demonstrates an increased risk of tendon degeneration/tears among first- and second-
degree relatives.15 Genetics may play a role in collagen composition, vasculature,
intracellular signaling, and the ability to regenerate native enthesis. Patients may be
genetically predisposed to healing with increased type III collagen compared with type I
collagen, resulting in more scar tissue production. Diabetes mellitus and high cholesterol
have been linked to poorer healing responses after rotator cuff repair. Bone has inferior
healing in patients with diabetes mellitus, which impairs tendon-bone healing. Patients
with diabetes mellitus also have compromised vascularity, which contributes to
accelerated tendon degeneration and reduced healing. In patients with high cholesterol,
deposits may develop in the tendon that may alter its mechanical strength and increase
the risk of injury or impair healing. This also may inhibit blood flow (Figure 6). A low
vitamin D level may be related to increased fatty infiltration of muscle.

Progression of Tendon Degeneration and Tears
Patient-reported outcomes may improve after nonsurgical management via physical therapy
in patients with a symptomatic full-thickness rotator cuff tear; however, tear size, muscle
atrophy, and fatty infiltration may progress over 5 to 10 years.20 Small full-thickness rotator
cuff tears and painful partial-thickness rotator cuff tears may substantially enlarge within 3 to
4 years; larger lesions progress faster and pose a higher risk for degenerative muscle changes.

Contrary to previous belief that most tears begin just posterior to the biceps, this more
posterior area correlates with the junction of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus, or is
predominantly infraspinatus, depending on the anatomic definition. In addition, this
correlates with the midpoint of the rotator crescent. This thinner, more avascular tissue
lateral to the rotator cable is more prone to tears, propagating anteriorly or posteriorly
from this position. The anterior attachment of the rotator cable typically is spared.
Tear Progression and Pain Development
Tears tend to progress anteriorly or posteriorly from the position 15 mm posterior to the
biceps tendon.
Studies regarding tear progression and the development of pain are conflicting, with some
studies suggesting that tear size correlates with progression and pain and other studies
showing no relation.
Disruption of the anterior supraspinatus is associated with greater tear size and degeneration,
likely from disruption of the rotator cable; however, anterior tendon integrity has shown no
effect on baseline function, postoperative function, or tendon healing.
Proximal humerus migration may occur if a tear reaches the critical area of 175 mm2,
correlating with a tear size of 15 mm and retraction of 12 to 15 mm.11

Tear Progression and Pain Development
The risk of partial-thickness tears enlarging at 2 and 5 years is 11% and 35%,
respectively, whereas full-thickness tears have a 22% and 50% risk of enlarging at 2 and
5 years, respectively.11 The Multicenter Orthopaedic Outcomes Network study
demonstrated that pain and duration of symptoms do not correlate with the size of the
tear, whereas other studies have suggested that full-thickness tears, as they progress in
size, become more symptomatic and result in more muscle degeneration compared with
smaller and partial-thickness tears. Studies have shown that tear enlargement and pain
are associated with hand dominance, suggesting that activity level may play a role.
Although pain is associated with tear progression, it is not an absolute symptom.15

In a prospective longitudinal study, Keener et al21 evaluated the long-term risk of tear
enlargement in asymptomatic rotator cuff tears by evaluating patients with an
asymptomatic tear who had a contralateral painful tear. The authors showed that tear
enlargement occurred in 49% of patients, with the median time to enlargement being 2.8
years. More severe (full-thickness) tears were prone to enlargement, symptom
development, and muscle degeneration. Cable-disrupted tears tend to be larger at
baseline than cable-intact tears (median, 19 mm versus 10 mm, respectively) but
demonstrate no difference in the risk of enlargement or time to enlargement. Cable-
intact tears tend to propagate anteriorly and posteriorly, whereas cable-disrupted tears
propagate posteriorly.22
Fatty Infiltration and Muscle Degeneration
The size and location of tears have been associated with muscle degeneration and fatty
infiltration.
Muscle degeneration is associated with full-thickness tears rather than partial-thickness tears.
Fatty degeneration is more common in older patients and those with larger baseline tears.
Rotator cuff tears with fatty degeneration are more prone to enlarging over time.

Fatty Infiltration and Muscle Degeneration
With prospective yearly evaluation, the median time of progression of muscle changes
after tear enlargement is 1 year for supraspinatus tears and 1.1 years for infraspinatus
tears; however, the timing is highly variable.23 Retrospective clinical studies have
suggested the onset of clinically relevant fatty muscle infiltration occurs 3 years after the
onset of symptoms within the supraspinatus compared with 2.5 years after the onset of
symptoms within the infraspinatus.23,24 Disruption of the anterior cable has been
associated with accelerated retraction and supraspinatus degeneration, suggesting that
size and location correlate with fatty infiltration. Larger sagittal plane tears are
associated with infraspinatus degeneration.4 The more anterior the tear, the higher risk
of tendon retraction and muscle atrophy. Advanced degeneration is linked to lower rates
of tendon healing.

Hebert-Davies et al25 evaluated patients with an asymptomatic rotator cuff tear in one
shoulder and pain from rotator cuff disease in the contralateral shoulder. After following
up with patients annually for a minimum of 2 years, the authors determined that fatty
degeneration was more common in older patients and those with larger baseline tears.
In addition, rotator cuff tears with fatty degeneration were more prone to enlarging over
time and were more likely to enlarge to a greater degree. If tears had enlarged, fatty
progression occurred more quickly and the tears were more likely to extend to the
anterior supraspinatus.
Basic Science of Tendon Tears, Repair, and Healing
Mechanism of Injury
Progression of Tendon Degeneration and Tears
Tendon injuries may result from direct trauma, such as a stab wound, or indirect injuries from
forceful loading of the muscle-tendon-bone unit to the point of tendon failure.
Degeneration is thought to involve hypoxia, ischemic damage, oxidative stress, nonuniform
mechanical loading, and the production of inflammatory cytokines (Figure 8).
As tendon degeneration progresses, muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration result from failed
muscle regeneration (not degeneration).
Degenerative rotator cuff tears are a spectrum of disease that beings with tendinitis;
progresses to tendinosis; subsequently results in tears; and if not managed, evolves to cuff
arthropathy.
Inflammation may be present in the earliest stages; however, most studies suggest that true
inflammation is absent.
Articular-sided tears are more common than bursal-sided tears.
Full-thickness tears often are separated by tear size, with those involving more than one
tendon and those larger than 2 to 3 cm considered large tears.
Over time, altered shoulder biomechanics and rotator cuff fatty infiltration leads to
degenerative changes in the shoulder, known as rotator cuff arthropathy.

Progression of Tendon Degeneration and Tears
Eccentric contraction is the most common cause of tendon injury. As patients age and
tendon properties weaken, the force required to cause a tear decreases. Metal
metalloproteinase (MMP) activity is positively correlated with tendon degradation and
rupture, and inhibitors may aid in tendon healing. Greater synovial inflammation and
degeneration is associated with greater tear severity. As tendon degradation progresses,
increasing amounts of hypoxia-inducible factor-1a are present and increased apoptosis
occurs. Similarly, increased vessel density is related to the amount of tendon retraction.
Overall, multifactorial cellular/molecular mechanisms predispose an individual to injury.7
The altered load-carrying properties and strain patterns in torn tendons mechanically
predispose patients to progression of tears and subsequent increased muscle atrophy
and fatty infiltration.

Tendinitis is caused by angiogenic and inflammatory imbalances that predispose
individuals to the earliest stages of tendinopathy, with evidence demonstrating that
inflammation may exist in its earliest stages. Tendinosis has largely replaced the term
tendinitis to describe chronic overuse injury because histologic studies have shown that
true inflammation generally is absent. Histologic specimens show disrupted and
disorganized collagen, increased extracellular matrix, increased tenocyte population,
and neovascularization. Although these changes initially occur in the hypovascular zone,
increasing the risk of more severe injury, such as rupture, hypervascularization occurs
later in tendinopathy.3 The articular side of the rotator cuff tendons has a greater
modulus of elasticity, decreased vascularity, and higher eccentric forces than the bursal
side, possibly causing partial articular tears to be more common than bursal-sided tears;
however, bursal-sided tears are more likely to occur in younger patients and may be
related to mechanical impingement. Bursal-sided tears may be more likely to progress to
full-thickness tears. A partial-thickness tear affects the load-carrying properties of the
residual rotator cuff tendon, predisposing the patient to further tear enlargement.26 To
increase remodeling and neovascularization, full-thickness tears demonstrate increased
proinflammatory cytokines and angiogenic factors compared with partial-thickness
tears.
Full-thickness tears are classified based on the amount of uncovered tuberosity; tears
less than 1 cm are classified as small, tears that are 1 to 3 cm are considered medium,
and tears that are 3 to 5 cm are considered large. Alternatively, tears involving one
tendon may be considered medium, whereas tears involving two or more tendons are
considered large. Fatty muscle infiltration occurs more quickly in tears involving more
than one tendon.27 Depending on the location of the tear, intact force couples may be
able to compensate and preserve reasonable shoulder function. After a critical tear area
of 175 mm2 is reached, superior migration of the humeral head from the unopposed
pull of the deltoid occurs, which may progress to mechanical erosions on the inferior
acromion and superior glenoid articular surface. Unmanaged massive tears increase in
size and fatty infiltration as the acromiohumeral interval continues to diminish. Over
time, cartilage wear, arthritis, and progressive glenoid and humeral head bony changes
may occur—a process known as cuff arthropathy.14 The timeline for the progression of
cuff tear arthropathy has not been fully elucidated. Increased muscle atrophy and

Tendon Repair and Healing
25% of rotator cuff tendon repairs do not heal; healing is affected by patient age, tendon
retraction, and fatty muscle infiltration, with most failure occurring during active rehabilitation
(2 to 3 months postoperatively).5
The repaired enthesis is weaker than normal tendon enthesis, with reactive scar formation
resulting in tissue that is biologically and mechanically inferior to native tissue.
The enthesis is formed by fibrocartilage insertion via four zones: tendon, unmineralized
fibrocartilage, mineralized fibrocartilage, and bone.
Pathologic changes of bone at the enthesis contribute to poor tendon healing.
Preparing the bone insertion site helps improve bone-tendon healing.
Midsubstance repair and healing generates well-aligned collagen fibers and may result in good
return of function.

Tendon Repair and Healing
The goal of repair is to restore the anatomic footprint and encourage healing; however,
patient age, fatty muscle degeneration, and atrophy alter the biologic healing response
and predispose patients to repair failure. Repair failure typically occurs at the tendon
attachment site, with the tendon pulling through the sutures. The repair site heals with a
fibrovascular scar at the tendon-bone interface, which has inferior histologic
microstructure and biomechanical properties (Figures 9 and 10). The interface is slow to
heal because of impaired biologic response and tendon vascularity. Increasing the
strength of the repair construct results in higher tendon healing rates, especially for
tears larger than 3 cm. Stronger repair constructs may better allow for safe early range
of motion. The timeline for mature rotator cuff tendon healing in humans is unknown;
however, many surgeons feel that progressive strengthening of the rotator cuff is safe 3
to 4 months after repair. Tendon repair integrity correlates with recovery of shoulder
strength but has not been consistently correlated with functional outcome. Actual

present at the tuberosity. Abnormal trabecular structure leads to weaker strength at the

any medical comorbidities that contribute to poor bone may be associated with poor
healing.7 Postoperatively, most blood flow to the rotator cuff repair site arises from the

increasing local blood flow to the repair site from the bone. Leaving the footprint
unmanaged or performing microfracture creates a repair with a greater mean load to
failure, thicker collagen bundles, and greater fibrocartilage formation in healed tissue.7
Radiofrequency ablation or excavation to cancellous bone results in poor healing.

Many variables impair rotator cuff tendon healing on the tendon and the bone side, such as
their intra-articular (intrasynovial) location, complex mechanical loading, native
fibrocartilaginous insertion, and element of chronic tendinopathy.
The stages of tendon healing include the inflammatory, proliferative, and remodeling stages.
After repair, an initial increase in growth factors occurs with the inflammatory response. This
is initiated by a proliferation of cells from the epitenon, followed by a proliferation of matrix

The degenerative tendon has a decreased ability to heal because of decreased collagen

The Science of Tendon Healing
The degenerative tendon has a reduced ability to heal because of decreased collagen
organization, increased cellularity, more rounded cells, and decreased mechanical
properties. The tenocytes secrete larger and more mature collagen (MMPs contribute).
Factors that reduce tendon healing include poor vascularity, excessive inflammatory
mediators/MMPs, and chronic tendinopathic changes. Tears have lower vascular volume
and lower resting perfusion at the insertion site. Two different types of healing occur:
intrinsic and extrinsic. Intrinsic healing causes a proliferation of cells in the tissue (ie,
tenocytes), improving the biomechanics of the tendon. Extrinsic healing occurs via the
invasion of cells from the surrounding sheath/synovium and leads to scar formation.
This is the predominant type of healing that occurs with rupture.30 Healed tendon is
composed of scar tissue, more type III collagen, smaller diameter of collagen fibers, and
abnormal collagen cross-linking. In tendon healing, a balance of pro-inflammatory and
anti-inflammatory mediators are present. More proapoptotic mediators are expressed
closer to the tendon edge, and more anti-apoptotic mediators are located farther from
the tendon edge.

The glenohumeral abduction angle and supraspinatus tendon loads are predictors of
infraspinatus and supraspinatus tendon strains. Therefore, tear and/or repair strain can
be reduced by limiting external loading and maintaining the shoulder in 30° of abduction
and in neutral rotation.7 Optimal loading influences healing by increasing growth factors
(at 8 weeks). Loading helps restore mechanical alignment of healing tissue and enhances
cell proliferation and tenocyte-related genes; however, a concentration of biomechanical
load at the suture/tendon interface may impair healing. Excessive load in the early
postoperative period impairs healing because the inflammatory response is not
complete. Excessive early loading inhibits healing because of poor collagen organization
and disorganized excessive scar formation, leading to a weaker bone-tendon interface;
however, prolonged immobilization may be detrimental by increasing local MMP13,
which weakens the bone-tendon complex. Therefore, temporary immobilization may be
beneficial in early healing. Immobilization improves collagen organization after 4 weeks
but not after 16 weeks. Immobilization allows for more organized repair, which improves
the early mechanical properties of the repair but must be balanced against the risk of
joint contracture. Although stiffness is more likely to occur if the shoulder is immobilized,
6 weeks of immobilization does not affect stiffness after 3 months.7
